claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure comprising dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has coarse lamellar spacing.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause localized stress concentrations in the starting alloy.
The boundary-associated stress concentrations promote brittle fracture during tensile loading.
The proposed intervention is high-strain-rate rolling followed by brief annealing.
Processing at approximately 0.4–0.5 of the homologous temperature is below the recrystallization temperature.
The processing sequence includes rapid cooling after rolling and annealing.
High-strain-rate rolling followed by brief annealing will refine the lamellar spacing.
The treatment will modify internal-boundary morphology so that dislocations are distributed more uniformly.
High-strain-rate rolling disrupts continuous internal boundaries.
Lamellar refinement and boundary disruption reduce dislocation accumulation at internal phase boundaries.
Reduced dislocation accumulation mitigates local stress concentrations and delays microcrack initiation.
Brief annealing stabilizes the refined microstructure without significant coarsening.
Avoiding significant coarsening during annealing helps maintain or enhance strength.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will retain or modestly increase strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The predicted improvement applies under quasi-static tensile loading at room temperature.
Processing outside the proposed intensity or duration window may activate alternative embrittlement mechanisms and limit improvement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the treatment a 'single-step' process, but the stated intervention contains two sequential operations: rolling and annealing.
